newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed against major currencies.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed against major currencies.

text.p: The dollar rose against the yen Monday despite signs the strong dollar is helping Japanese exporters. It ended lower against the German mark after a barrage of comments by German central bankers.

Japan's merchandise trade surplus with the United States grew in October for the first time since February 1995, after a weak yen led Japanese automobile manufacturers to increase exports, Japan's Finance Ministry said on Monday.
A rising Japanese surplus risks increased trade friction with the United States and would usually weigh on the dollar as Japan accumulates surplus U.S. currency from the sale of exports.

Instead, the yen weakened broadly because the overall Japanese trade surplus shrank 12.9 percent in October from a year earlier. The bilateral surplus with the United States rose 31.3 percent to almost 355 billion yen ($3.18 billion).

"You had the Japanese trade figure on the whole showing improvement year-on-year, but the key area with the U.S. registered as quite a disappointment to the market," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole.
The dollar rose to 111.53 yen late in New York from 111.07 late on Friday.

The dollar fell to 1.5020 marks from 1.5093 marks, hurt mainly by wire service reports that Ernst Welteke, a Council Member of the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, said he saw no reason for the dollar to appreciate at this time.

After dipping under 1.50 marks, the dollar reclaimed some ground as Welteke said the reports got his comments wrong, telling journalists the Bundesbank wanted to see a "more stable" and "stronger" dollar.

"It's just contrary statements pushing the dollar back and forth," said John Nelson, a senior vice president at ABN-Amro Bank in Chicago, noting that the dollar trading was otherwise uneventful against the mark.

Traders said the dollar started weakening in Europe, when the mark firmed after Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler warned Eurpean countries not to use creative accounting to meet tough fiscal conditions for joining Europe's single currency in 1999.

The mark, currently Europe's anchor currency, is scheduled to be replaced by a weaker single currency, called the euro, in 1999. The German unit often strengthens when tensions threaten to delay progress towards currency union.

The mark gave little back against the dollar after a third Bundesbank member, Hans-Juergen Krupp, said the guidelines for participation in the single currency do not require budget deficit and public debt targets to be hit exactly.
"There are obviously two different sides of the story, even out of the Bundesbank," said David Solin, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"The question is how much input does the Bundesbank really have into this process? I think when push comes to shove it's a political issue, not a monetary issue."
In other trading, the British pound rose to a fresh four-year high of $1.6710 from $1.6635 on Friday.
The dollar fell to 1.2675 Swiss francs from 1.2792.
It rose to Canadian $1.3428 from C$1.3388 late Friday.
